label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
D. Bergeron — you deserve a straight answer, and you deserve it before January 4. I’m sorry that my vague little sign made people worry instead. So here it is, with no surprise and no mystery:

**We are not closing, and we are not moving. I bought the building.**

Boulangerie Le Pétrin Doré has been at our corner at 5 rue Fairmount since March 2009, and I intend for it to stay there. We signed at the notary on December 15. It is now official.

M. Ferland, who owned the building, is 81. He is retiring to Sherbrooke to be with his daughter. Before offering the building to anyone else, he offered to sell it to me. For 17 years, he has come in every morning for his *baguette pas trop cuite*. He cried a little at the notary’s office. This was not just a transaction between strangers, and buying his building means a great deal to me.

So, Marc-Antoine, your cousin is half right: the building was sold. But it was sold to me — not to someone planning to replace the bakery with condos, a bank or a vape shop. I bought it so that we could stay and finally make a few improvements.

The work is why we will be closed **from January 4 through January 18**. We will reopen on **Tuesday, January 19, at 7 a.m.**

Our current oven dates from 1998 and has broken down three times this year. A baker cannot keep crossing her fingers every morning and hoping the oven will cooperate. We are replacing it with a new four-deck oven from a supplier in Laval. That is a big investment for a small bakery, and it is not something you do when you are planning to disappear.

We are also taking over the space at the back, the old storage area of the dépanneur. We will put in six small tables. They will not be fancy, but finally people will be able to sit down with a coffee and something to eat instead of always taking everything away.

Now, about the carnets, because this is the part I want to make absolutely clear.

In October, we sold 214 carnets. Each one cost $60 and was good for 12 loaves. **Every carnet is still valid. All the remaining loaves will be honoured, and there is no expiry date.** Nothing about buying the building or closing for the work changes that.

To the person who wrote that they still have seven loaves left: those seven loaves are still yours. You will be able to use them after we reopen, exactly as you could before.

Every carnet holder will also receive **one free croissant in January**, as a thank-you for your patience during the closure. And if someone truly prefers to have their money back for a carnet rather than keep it, come and see me. I will refund it, with no questions and no hard feelings. I would rather do that than have even one person feel that I took advantage of their trust.

The carnets were not a scheme to collect money before closing. I understand why the timing looked strange once people saw the sign and heard that the building had been sold. But I will be honest: reading the word “scam” after 17 years on this street hurt. I know most of our customers by face, many by name, and some of your children have grown up coming through our door. I am not disappearing with anybody’s bread money.

As for the sign, my nephew Thomas wrote it at 6 o’clock in the morning. “Grande nouvelle bientôt!” was his idea. He was excited about the building, the oven and the tables, and I said yes without properly thinking about how it would sound to someone reading it on the door. That was my mistake, not his. It never occurred to me that “big news” would sound like “goodbye.” I should simply have written that we were closing for renovations and reopening on January 19. I’m sorry for causing all this anxiety with three careless words.

The half-empty shelves on the 28th were also not a sign that we were clearing out the bakery. They were the aftermath of Christmas. We sold everything for Christmas Eve, including 400 bûches. It was a very busy holiday, not a quiet liquidation.

I also want to reassure the people living upstairs, because this has probably not been pleasant for them to read either. **The three apartments will remain rented to the same tenants, at the same rent.** I have promised them that in writing. Nobody is being asked to leave because of my purchase. They do not need to worry that the bakery’s good news is bad news for them.

I understand why people in Mile End react quickly when a small business puts up a closed sign. We have lost too many neighbourhood shops, and usually the first rumours turn out to contain at least some bad news. Your concern comes from caring about the street, and I am not looking for a fight with anyone over it. But this time, the news really is good. I just did a poor job of announcing it.

Priya, thank you for what you wrote. Thank you also to everyone else who defended us, reminded people of our history, or simply waited for an answer instead of assuming the worst. It meant more to me than you probably realize. And thank you as well to those who asked difficult questions politely. You have paid for bread in advance, and you are entitled to know exactly where things stand.

I had hoped to keep everything as a surprise for the reopening, but I would rather spoil my own surprise than leave my neighbours worrying.

So please consider this your invitation. We reopen for regular business on **Tuesday, January 19, at 7 a.m.** Then, on **Saturday, January 23**, come and celebrate with us. Everyone is welcome — regulars, carnet holders, neighbours, upstairs tenants, and yes, the people who were suspicious too. I will have **free coffee and a free piece of bread from the new oven** for you.

Come see the oven, find a seat at one of the new tables, and let me thank you in person. After all these years, the best news I can give Mile End is very simple: we are staying.

Hélène Gagnon  
Boulangerie Le Pétrin Doré  
5 rue Fairmount
